meta.titre: Meiosis and Variation: from one diploid cell to four different gametes
meta.sous_theme: Stages of meiosis and sources of variation

sections.contenu_markdown: Two children of the same parents in a family in Bafoussam can differ in height, skin tone and blood group, even though they got their genes from the same two people. A farmer who saves maize seed notices that no two plants in the field are exactly alike. The cause is meiosis, the special cell division that makes gametes, together with random fertilisation. GCE papers test your ability to describe the stages, to compare meiosis with mitosis, to link meiosis to the life cycle of flowering plants and to explain how variation arises.

items: Diploid cells ($2n$) have two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent; haploid cells ($n$) have one set.
In mitosis one cell divides once to give two genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
Each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids after DNA replication in interphase.
Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci but may carry different alleles.

sections.titre: Meiosis, its stages and the variation it creates
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Meiosis** is the division of a diploid cell that gives **four haploid cells**, each genetically different. It consists of two divisions, **meiosis I** and **meiosis II**, after one DNA replication in interphase.

**Meiosis I (reduction division).**
- **Prophase I:** chromosomes condense; homologous chromosomes pair up in **synapsis** to form **bivalents**; **crossing over** takes place between non-sister chromatids at **chiasmata**; the nuclear envelope breaks down.
- **Metaphase I:** bivalents line up on the equator, the orientation of each pair being random (**independent assortment**).
- **Anaphase I:** whole chromosomes of each homologous pair separate and move to opposite poles; the centromeres do not divide.
- **Telophase I:** two haploid cells form, each with chromosomes that still have two chromatids.

**Meiosis II.** It resembles mitosis in a haploid cell. In metaphase II the chromosomes line up singly; in **anaphase II** the centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate; four haploid cells result.

| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Number of divisions | One | Two |
| Daughter cells | Two, diploid, identical | Four, haploid, different |
| Pairing of homologues (bivalents) | No | Yes, in prophase I |
| Crossing over | No | Yes |
| Role | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gamete or spore formation; sexual life cycles |

**Sources of variation.** (1) **Crossing over** in prophase I; (2) **independent assortment** of homologous pairs in metaphase I, giving $2^n$ different chromosome combinations in a gamete (where $n$ is the haploid number) without counting crossing over; (3) **random fertilisation** of one gamete by another, so the number of combinations in the zygote is $(2^n)^2=2^{2n}$; (4) **mutation**, which creates new alleles. Errors in meiosis such as non-disjunction (failure of homologues or chromatids to separate) give gametes with an extra or missing chromosome.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about spore formation and where meiosis occurs in a flower.
variantes.contenu_markdown: In the **anther**, diploid pollen mother cells divide by meiosis to form four haploid **microspores**, each becoming a pollen grain. In the **ovule**, a diploid **megaspore mother cell** in the nucellus divides by meiosis to form four haploid **megaspores**. Three degenerate and one survives; its nucleus divides by mitosis three times to give eight haploid nuclei in the embryo sac, including the egg cell and two polar nuclei. In double fertilisation one male nucleus fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote and another fuses with the polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm nucleus.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives the diploid number and asks for numbers at a stage.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Count centromeres to count chromosomes. Take $2n=12$: prophase I has 12 chromosomes (24 chromatids) forming 6 bivalents; anaphase I has 6 chromosomes (12 chromatids) moving to each pole; metaphase II has 6 chromosomes (12 chromatids) in each cell; anaphase II has 12 chromosomes (each now one chromatid) in each cell, 6 at each pole; the final four cells each have 6 chromosomes.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked how many different gametes or zygotes are possible.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Ignoring crossing over, one gamete type for each way of orienting $n$ bivalents gives $2^n$ gametes. Two parents give $2^n\times 2^n=2^{2n}$ different zygotes. Crossing over increases these numbers enormously.

sections.enonce_markdown: Maize has a diploid number of 20 chromosomes. Ignoring crossing over, calculate the number of different chromosome combinations that one plant can make in its gametes, and the number of genetically different zygotes possible when two plants are crossed. State the number of chromosomes in a pollen nucleus and in the endosperm.

etapes.justification: A gamete receives one chromosome of each homologous pair, so $n = 2n \div 2$.
Each of the $n$ bivalents may orient in 2 ways in metaphase I, and the orientations are independent, so the combinations multiply.
Any gamete from one parent can fuse with any gamete from the other parent.
A pollen nucleus is haploid; the endosperm nucleus comes from fusion of a male nucleus with two polar nuclei, all haploid, so it is triploid.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Pollen nucleus: 10 chromosomes. Endosperm nucleus: $3n=30$ chromosomes.

sections.conclusion_markdown: One maize plant can make 1024 different chromosome combinations in its gametes, giving 1 048 576 possible zygotes from two plants even before crossing over and mutation are counted.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase II.
items.pourquoi_faux: Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I. In anaphase II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.
items.correction_markdown: Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate (reduction). Anaphase II: sister chromatids separate.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that meiosis produces four identical haploid cells.
items.pourquoi_faux: The four cells are genetically different because of crossing over and independent assortment.
items.correction_markdown: Say four haploid cells that differ genetically from each other and from the parent cell.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that crossing over occurs in metaphase I.
items.pourquoi_faux: Crossing over takes place in prophase I, when the homologues are paired as bivalents. Independent assortment is the event of metaphase I.
items.correction_markdown: Name prophase I for crossing over and metaphase I for independent assortment.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that the megaspore mother cell is haploid and divides by mitosis to form megaspores.
items.pourquoi_faux: The megaspore mother cell is diploid and divides by meiosis to give four haploid megaspores, only one of which survives.
items.correction_markdown: Diploid megaspore mother cell $\xrightarrow{\text{meiosis}}$ four haploid megaspores.

items.erreur_markdown: Using $2n$ instead of $2^n$ for the number of possible gametes.
items.pourquoi_faux: Each bivalent has two possible orientations independent of the others, so the possibilities multiply, giving a power of 2.
items.correction_markdown: Number of different gametes $=2^n$, with $n$ the haploid number.

items.enonce_markdown: An onion has a diploid number of 16. (a) How many chromosomes are present in a gamete cell? (b) How many different combinations of chromosomes can be formed in its gametes, ignoring crossing over?

A fruit fly has a diploid number of 8. (a) Calculate the number of different gamete types, ignoring crossing over. (b) Calculate the number of zygote types from a cross of two such flies. (c) Name two processes, other than independent assortment, that increase the variation among the offspring.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $n = 4$, so $2^4 =$ **16** gamete types.

(b) $16 \times 16 =$ **256** zygote types.

(c) Any two of: crossing over in prophase I; mutation; random fertilisation, since any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete.

items.enonce_markdown: A cell has a diploid number of 12. (a) State the number of chromosomes and of chromatids in one cell at (i) prophase I, (ii) the end of anaphase I at one pole, (iii) metaphase II, (iv) the end of meiosis II. (b) Calculate the probability that a gamete contains only the six chromosomes that came from the mother of the organism, ignoring crossing over. (c) Explain why the cells at the end of meiosis I are already haploid, though sister chromatids have not yet separated.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) (i) 12 chromosomes and 24 chromatids (6 bivalents). (ii) 6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids at each pole. (iii) 6 chromosomes and 12 chromatids in each cell. (iv) 6 chromosomes and 6 chromatids in each of the four cells.

(b) Each of the six pairs has a probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of contributing the maternal chromosome. $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^6 = \dfrac{1}{64} =$ **0.0156**.

(c) Homologous chromosomes were separated in anaphase I, so each cell has only one chromosome of each pair (6 centromeres). A cell is haploid when it has one chromosome of each type, even if each chromosome still has two chromatids.

items_markdown: Meiosis is two divisions after one replication; it produces four genetically different haploid cells from one diploid cell.
Homologous chromosomes pair and cross over in prophase I, line up randomly in metaphase I and separate in anaphase I; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
Variation arises from crossing over, independent assortment ($2^n$ gamete types), random fertilisation and mutation.
In flowering plants a diploid megaspore mother cell gives four haploid megaspores of which three degenerate; microspores form pollen grains.
Meiosis differs from mitosis in two divisions, pairing of homologues, crossing over, four haploid and different daughter cells.
